title: Permutation in String
directAnswer: Return true if s2 contains a substring that is a permutation (anagram) of s1. Since any permutation of s1 has the same length and character counts, slide a fixed-size window of length |s1| across s2 and check whether the window's character counts match s1's. Maintain the counts incrementally with a 'matches' counter. O(|s2|) time, O(1) space (26 counts).

remember.pattern: Fixed-size sliding window of frequency counts
remember.formula:
if len(s1) > len(s2): return False
need, win = [0]*26, [0]*26
for c in s1: need[c]++ 
for i in range(len(s1)): win[s2[i]]++
if win == need: return True
for i in range(len(s1), len(s2)):
    win[s2[i]] += 1
    win[s2[i-len(s1)]] -= 1
    if win == need: return True
return False
rules: A permutation has the **same length and same character counts** — order is irrelevant.
The window is **fixed-size** at |s1|; slide by adding the new char and removing the one that falls off.
Compare counts, not strings — a 26-length count array comparison is O(1).
A `matches`/`required` counter avoids re-comparing all 26 slots each slide for true O(|s2|).
whenToUse: Detect an anagram/permutation as a contiguous substring
The target window size is known and fixed
Equality of multisets can be tracked incrementally as the window slides
Fixed-length 'does this pattern appear (reordered)' substring problems
antiSignals: Window size varies with a constraint → variable sliding window (LC3, LC76)
t must appear in order → substring search (KMP), not anagram matching
Need all matching positions → same window, collect indices (LC438)
remember.takeaway: When the target length is fixed, a fixed-size sliding window of character counts answers anagram-presence in one pass. Add-one / remove-one count maintenance plus a matches counter is the template — it extends directly to Find All Anagrams.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that a permutation is just an equal-multiset, equal-length match, and use a fixed-size sliding window of counts updated incrementally rather than re-sorting or recounting each window.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-sorting or rebuilding the count map for every window (O(|s1|) per slide), or forgetting the add-and-remove pairing so the window drifts off its fixed size.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the sort-each-window brute force, then 'counts must match and lengths are equal, so a fixed window of frequencies sliding in O(1) per step works'. Mention the matches counter for strict O(|s2|).

problemStatement:
Given two strings `s1` and `s2`, return `true` if `s2` contains a **permutation** of `s1`, or `false` otherwise.

In other words, return `true` if one of `s1`'s permutations is a **substring** of `s2`.
constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters
understanding: A permutation of s1 is any reordering of its characters, so it has exactly s1's length and exactly s1's character frequencies. The task reduces to: does any length-|s1| substring of s2 have the same character counts as s1? That's a fixed-size window scan.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the permutation have to be contiguous in s2?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — it must appear as a substring (a contiguous block), not a scattered subsequence.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What defines a permutation match?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Same length and identical character frequencies as s1; order doesn't matter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if s1 is longer than s2?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No window of length |s1| fits in s2, so return false immediately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the alphabet?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase English letters — a fixed 26-slot count array, so space is O(1).

examples.explanation: s2 contains "ba" at indices 3–4, which is a permutation of "ab".
No length-2 window of s2 has counts {a:1, b:1}.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: A fixed-size window of counts is the default; sorting or recounting each window is the slower baseline.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recount Every Window
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the baseline and to make 'permutation = equal counts' explicit.
hints: A permutation of s1 has the same length as s1. So only substrings of s2 of length |s1| can match.
For each such window, count its characters (or sort it) and compare to s1's counts (or sorted s1).
Scan all windows and return true on the first match. Each window recount is O(|s1|) — that's the inefficiency to remove.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are O(|s2|) windows; counting each from scratch is O(|s1|), giving O(|s2|·|s1|). The count arrays are fixed 26 ints → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Build the frequency count of `s1`. Then for every start index `i` in `s2` such that a length-|s1| window fits, count the characters of `s2[i .. i+|s1|-1]` and compare to `s1`'s counts. Return true on the first window whose counts match.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** It hinges on the key realization: a permutation is exactly an equal-length, equal-frequency match. Once you see that, comparing counts per window is the obvious correct method (sorting each window and comparing strings is an equivalent, slightly slower variant).

**Why we don't ship this.** Recounting each window from scratch ignores that consecutive windows overlap in all but two characters. With |s1| and |s2| up to 10⁴, the O(|s2|·|s1|) product is wasteful. Sliding the window and updating only the entering and leaving character makes each step O(1).
approaches.insight: Adjacent windows differ by exactly one character added on the right and one dropped on the left. Recounting the whole window throws that away; incremental count maintenance is the entire optimization.

dryRun.intro: need = {a:1,b:1}. Count each length-2 window and compare.

java.explanation: No window of length |s1| fits — early exit.

java.line: for (int j = i; j < i + len; j++) win[s2.charAt(j) - 'a']++;
java.explanation: Recount the whole window — the O(|s1|) per-step waste.
Matching counts means this window is a permutation of s1.

python.line:
for j in range(i, i + length):
            win[ord(s2[j]) - ord('a')] += 1
python.explanation: Rebuild the window count each time — slow.

pitfalls: Recounting each window instead of sliding — the O(|s1|) per-step cost.
Comparing as sorted strings repeatedly, which is even slower (O(|s1| log |s1|) per window).
Missing the |s1| > |s2| early exit, risking out-of-range windows.

approaches.name: Fixed-Size Sliding Window of Counts (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'slide a window of length |s1|, adding the entering char and removing the leaving one, comparing counts'.
hints: Both the target length (|s1|) and the comparison (equal counts) are fixed. Build s1's count array and an initial window of the first |s1| chars of s2.
Slide the window one step at a time: add the new right character's count and subtract the character that exits on the left. The window size stays |s1|.
To avoid re-comparing all 26 counts each slide, track a `matches` counter of how many of the 26 letters currently have equal counts in window and need; the window is a permutation when matches == 26.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the counts is O(|s1|). Sliding across s2 is O(|s2|) steps, each O(1) with the matches counter (or O(26) with array compare, still O(|s2|)). The two 26-slot arrays are O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Because every permutation of `s1` has length `|s1|`, the window size is fixed — we only ever look at length-`|s1|` slices of `s2`. Build `need` (s1's counts) and `window` (counts of the first `|s1|` characters of `s2`), then slide.

**Sliding in O(1) per step.** Moving the window one position right means exactly two changes: the new character at index `i` enters (increment its count) and the character at index `i − |s1|` leaves (decrement its count). The window's length is preserved automatically by always pairing one add with one remove. No recounting.

**Checking the match cheaply with a `matches` counter.** Comparing the two 26-length arrays every slide is O(26) — fine, and still O(|s2|) overall, but we can do strict O(1) per step. Keep `matches` = the number of letters `x` for which `window[x] == need[x]`. When we change a letter's window count, we look at whether that letter's equality flipped: if it was equal and now isn't, `matches--`; if it just became equal, `matches++`. The window is a permutation of `s1` exactly when `matches == 26`.

**Why equal counts is the whole test.** Two strings are permutations of each other iff they have identical character frequencies. Length equality is guaranteed by the fixed window, so frequency equality is both necessary and sufficient — no need to consider order at all.

**Why the early exit matters.** If `|s1| > |s2|`, no window fits and the answer is immediately false; this also prevents constructing an out-of-range initial window.

**Why O(|s2|) time and O(1) space.** Each character of `s2` enters and leaves the window at most once, and the only storage is two constant-size count arrays plus the matches counter.
approaches.insight: Fixing the window size collapses the problem to 'do these two frequency vectors match as the window slides?'. The add-one/remove-one update keeps each step O(1), and the `matches` counter turns the 26-way comparison into a single integer test — the same incremental-equality trick that solves Find All Anagrams.

dryRun.intro: Window length 2. Slide adding the entering char, removing the leaving char; check counts == need {a:1,b:1}.

java.explanation: Build s1's target counts and the initial length-|s1| window together.
Initialize matches = number of letters whose counts already agree.
Entering char; if its count just hit the target, one more letter matches.
Overshot the target → that letter no longer matches.
All 26 letters agree → the final window is a permutation of s1.

python.line: matches = sum(1 for x in range(26) if window[x] == need[x])
python.explanation: Count letters whose window and need counts already match.
Check before sliding so the initial window is tested too.
Add entering char; update matches if it reached the target.
Remove leaving char; it may newly match the target.

diagrams.title: Fixed window of width 2 sliding over s2
diagrams.caption: The window keeps length |s1|=2; each step adds the entering char and drops the leaving one.

diagrams.title: Window counts vs need
diagrams.caption: matches counts how many letters' window counts equal need. true when matches == 26.

edgeCases.behavior: Window of size 1 equals need immediately → returns true before any slide.
No length-3 window mixes a,b,c equally → returns false.

pitfalls: Forgetting to check matches/equality for the initial window before sliding (missing a match at index 0).
Updating matches with wrong threshold logic (the need[x] ± 1 boundary conditions).
Not pairing every add with a remove, letting the window size drift away from |s1|.

commonMistakes: Recounting or re-sorting each window instead of sliding incrementally.
Comparing windows as ordered strings rather than as character counts.
Forgetting to test the very first window before the slide loop begins.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Rebuilding the window each step
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adjacent windows overlap in all but two characters; recounting from scratch is O(|s1|) per step and defeats the point of a sliding window.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing strings instead of counts
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A permutation is defined by equal frequencies, not order. Sorting each window to compare is correct but slower than count comparison.

followupVariations.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
followupVariations.hint: Same fixed-size window, but collect every start index where counts match instead of returning on the first.

followupVariations.title: Minimum Window Substring
followupVariations.hint: Variable window that must cover (not equal) t — grow then shrink.

followupVariations.title: Valid Anagram
followupVariations.hint: The count-equality test without the window — just compare frequencies of two strings.

followupVariations.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
followupVariations.hint: Variable window with a distinctness constraint instead of a fixed-size count match.

patternNote: Fixed-size sliding window of frequency counts with incremental add/remove and a matches counter. Reach for it on anagram/permutation-presence problems where the window length is known. Same family as Find All Anagrams and Valid Anagram.
